claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially a high-temperature BCC phase.
The emergence of multiple phases during cooling and subsequent isothermal exposure is primarily controlled by competition between diffusion-limited elemental partitioning and local chemical ordering.
Lower-temperature thermal exposure can promote decomposition of an initially single-phase high-temperature state into multiple phases in the Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni alloy system.
Slow cooling allows diffusion-driven local chemical ordering and compositional fluctuations.
Slow cooling stimulates heterogeneous nucleation of secondary FCC or intermetallic phases.
Local chemical segregation lowers the barrier for heterogeneous nucleation of secondary phases.
Rapid quenching suppresses atomic migration and local chemical segregation.
Rapid quenching kinetically preserves the high-temperature BCC structure with minimal secondary-phase formation.
Slowly cooled samples will contain a statistically significant larger fraction of secondary-phase precipitates than rapidly quenched samples.
Slowly cooled samples will exhibit clearer local compositional fluctuations than rapidly quenched samples.
Subsequent isothermal holds will advance transformation more strongly in slowly cooled samples than in quenched samples.
The mechanism applies at intermediate temperatures where diffusion is appreciable but limited and when cooling rates produce appreciably different diffusion lengths.
The mechanism should not operate at temperatures too low for significant diffusion.
Mechanical stress or deformation-induced transformations can override the proposed diffusion-controlled behavior.
Local compositional variations should correlate temporally or spatially with the onset of secondary-phase nucleation.
